subsections.subsection_title: What the OSCE station may say

blocks.text: A 38-year-old woman presents with progressive abdominal swelling, heavy menstrual bleeding and pelvic pressure. A pelvic ultrasound reveals an enlarged uterus containing multiple masses. An MRI pelvis has been performed.
Tasks:
Interpret the MRI findings.
State the most likely diagnosis.
Give three differential diagnoses.
Outline further investigations and management.

A 29-year-old nulliparous woman presents with severe dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, chronic pelvic pain and difficulty conceiving. MRI pelvis demonstrates an ovarian lesion and abnormalities in the posterior pelvic compartment.
Tasks: Describe the findings, identify the likely diagnosis, explain the clinical significance and outline management.
A 52-year-old woman presents with postcoital bleeding and a biopsy-confirmed cervical carcinoma. MRI pelvis is requested to assess local tumour extent.
Tasks: Describe the imaging findings, identify features of parametrial invasion and explain how the findings influence treatment.
In an MRI interpretation station, the candidate is usually expected to interpret images rather than physically examine the patient.
If the station includes counselling or preparation for MRI, demonstrate appropriate communication.

“Good morning. I am one of the doctors looking after you. Your ultrasound has identified an abnormality in the pelvis, and we would like to perform an MRI scan to assess it in more detail. MRI uses a strong magnetic field and radiofrequency waves rather than ionising radiation. The scan will help us understand the location, size and characteristics of the abnormality so that we can plan appropriate treatment.”
Confirm patient identity and clinical indication.
Ask about cardiac devices, cochlear implants, aneurysm clips, neurostimulators and other metallic implants.
Ask about previous metal injuries, especially metallic fragments in the eyes.
Assess pregnancy possibility and gestational age where relevant.
Ask about claustrophobia and ability to lie still.
Ask about previous reactions to gadolinium contrast.
Assess renal function when indicated for contrast safety.
Explain that the scanner is noisy and that the patient may need to remain still for approximately 20–45 minutes, depending on the protocol.

Examiner tip: MRI without contrast may be performed during pregnancy when clinically indicated. Gadolinium is generally avoided during pregnancy unless its expected clinical benefit justifies the potential fetal risk.
Preparation depends on the indication and the imaging protocol.

Representative educational MRI references. In an examination, confirm the orientation and sequence from the displayed image labels.

On T2-weighted MRI in a reproductive-age woman, the uterus generally demonstrates three zones:
Normal appearances vary with age, menstrual phase, pregnancy and menopausal status.
Usually demonstrate multiple small follicles in reproductive-age patients.
Follicular fluid is typically hyperintense on T2.
No suspicious solid enhancing mass.
No concerning associated pelvic disease.

Low T2 signal of the fibrous cervical stroma.

“The uterus is normal in size and contour, with preserved myometrial architecture and junctional zone. The endometrial cavity is unremarkable. Both ovaries demonstrate normal morphology, with no suspicious adnexal masses. There is no pelvic lymphadenopathy or significant free fluid. Overall, no significant pelvic abnormality is identified.”

subsections.subsection_title: Abnormal MRI findings — high-yield OSCE cases

“This is a T2-weighted MRI of the pelvis demonstrating an enlarged uterus containing multiple well-circumscribed, predominantly low-signal myometrial masses. The largest is located within the anterior uterine wall and distorts the endometrial cavity. These findings are most consistent with multiple uterine leiomyomas.”
Adenomyosis or focal adenomyoma.
Uterine smooth muscle tumour of uncertain malignant potential.
Uterine leiomyosarcoma.
Other rare mesenchymal uterine tumours.
MRI may identify suspicious features, but it cannot reliably exclude leiomyosarcoma in every case.
Depends on symptoms, fibroid size and location, fertility preferences and suspicion of malignancy.

A junctional zone thickness of 12 mm or more is a classic supportive finding, but it is not diagnostic in isolation. Menstrual phase, age, hormonal therapy and other features must be considered.

Heavy menstrual bleeding.

Enlarged, sometimes tender uterus.

“The MRI demonstrates a globular enlarged uterus with diffuse thickening and poor definition of the junctional zone, associated with small cystic foci within the myometrium. These findings are suggestive of adenomyosis.”
Uterine fibroids.

content_groups.group_title: What is the T2 shading sign?

blocks.text: It describes loss of signal within a T1-hyperintense ovarian cyst on T2-weighted images, typically due to concentrated chronic haemorrhagic contents.

“There is a well-defined left ovarian cystic lesion demonstrating high signal intensity on T1-weighted imaging and reduced signal intensity on T2-weighted imaging, producing the characteristic T2 shading sign. The findings are highly suggestive of an ovarian endometrioma.”
Haemorrhagic ovarian cyst.
Dermoid cyst.
Haemorrhagic neoplasm.
Other blood-containing adnexal lesions.
Analgesia.
Hormonal suppression for pain when pregnancy is not being attempted.
Fertility assessment where relevant.
Specialist endometriosis referral for suspected deep disease.
Laparoscopic surgery for selected patients with persistent symptoms, concerning imaging or other indications.
Important fertility point: Ovarian endometrioma surgery can reduce ovarian reserve. Do not automatically recommend cystectomy for every patient, particularly before assisted reproduction.
Irregular low T2 signal fibrotic nodules.
Thickening of uterosacral ligaments.
Obliteration of the pouch of Douglas.
Adhesions and distorted pelvic anatomy.
Rectovaginal septum infiltration.
Rectosigmoid bowel wall involvement.
Possible ureteric involvement and hydronephrosis.

“The MRI demonstrates irregular low T2 signal nodular thickening in the posterior pelvic compartment, involving the uterosacral ligament and rectovaginal region, with associated distortion of the pouch of Douglas. These findings are suggestive of deep pelvic endometriosis.”
Why is MRI useful in deep endometriosis?
Model answer:

“MRI helps map the distribution and extent of deep endometriosis, particularly disease affecting the bowel, bladder, ureters and posterior pelvic compartment. This assists multidisciplinary surgical planning. However, a normal MRI does not exclude superficial peritoneal endometriosis.”
Analgesia and hormonal treatment when appropriate.
Specialist endometriosis assessment.
Multidisciplinary management for bowel, urinary tract or extensive disease.
Fertility-focused planning if pregnancy is desired.
Surgery when clinically indicated, balancing symptom relief against operative risks.
Intermediate-to-high T2 signal cervical mass.
Disruption of normal low-signal cervical stromal ring.

Restricted diffusion in the tumour.

Irregular or spiculated tumour margins extending into parametrial fat.
Encasement of parametrial vessels.
Associated ureteric obstruction in advanced cases.
Disruption of the stromal ring alone is not always sufficient to prove parametrial invasion.

“The MRI demonstrates an irregular cervical mass with intermediate-to-high T2 signal and restricted diffusion. There is disruption of the low-signal cervical stromal ring with extension into the adjacent parametrial tissue, suspicious for parametrial invasion. The findings are consistent with locally advanced cervical carcinoma in the context of the established biopsy diagnosis.”

“The MRI demonstrates an irregular endometrial mass with evidence of myometrial invasion. The findings are suspicious for endometrial carcinoma, and histopathological confirmation is required if not already obtained.”
Q: What is the role of MRI in endometrial cancer?
MRI is useful for evaluating myometrial invasion, cervical stromal involvement and local disease extent, which may influence treatment planning.
Q: What is the definitive diagnostic test?
Endometrial tissue sampling with histopathological examination.
Q: Does MRI determine the final FIGO stage?
Not by itself. Modern endometrial cancer staging incorporates surgical/pathological findings and, where available, molecular classification.

MRI can help distinguish congenital uterine anomalies by demonstrating both the endometrial cavity and external fundal contour.

rows: Internal uterine septum with relatively preserved external fundal contour
Two uterine horns with a significant external fundal cleft
Two separate uterine cavities and typically two cervices
Single developed uterine horn, sometimes with a rudimentary horn

blocks.text: Congenital uterine anomalies may be associated with recurrent pregnancy loss, preterm birth, malpresentation, infertility in some cases and obstructive reproductive tract symptoms.
Model answer:

“MRI demonstrates two endometrial cavities separated by a septum, with a relatively preserved external fundal contour, favouring a septate uterus. Further classification should use standardised uterine anomaly criteria.”
Examiner pearl: Do not confuse a septate uterus with a bicornuate uterus. The external fundal contour is crucial.

subsections.subsection_title: How to report MRI pelvis findings

blocks.text: The examiner may display an image and ask:

items: “Please describe this MRI and give your diagnosis.”

blocks.text: Use this standard format:
“This is a [plane] [sequence] MRI image of the female pelvis obtained for [clinical indication].
The uterus is [normal/enlarged] and demonstrates [relevant findings].
There is a [size] [solid/cystic/mixed] lesion arising from [site], with [signal characteristics], [margin characteristics] and [enhancement or diffusion findings, if demonstrated].
The lesion [does/does not] involve adjacent structures. The ovaries, bladder, rectum and pelvic lymph nodes demonstrate [findings].
Overall, the appearances are most consistent with [diagnosis].
Important differentials include [alternatives].
I would correlate these findings with the clinical presentation, formal radiology report and appropriate further investigations.”
Do not claim that a lesion enhances, restricts diffusion or lacks lymphadenopathy unless the displayed images or accompanying report actually demonstrate this.

items: High-yield viva questions with model answers

blocks.text: 1. What is the main advantage of MRI over ultrasound in gynaecology?MRI provides excellent soft-tissue contrast and multiplanar assessment. It is particularly useful for problem-solving, mapping deep endometriosis, characterising indeterminate adnexal masses and evaluating local tumour extent.

2. What is the classical MRI appearance of a uterine fibroid?A well-circumscribed myometrial mass that is usually low signal on T2-weighted images, with variable enhancement and signal changes if degeneration is present.
3. What is the T2 shading sign?Reduced T2 signal in a T1-hyperintense cyst due to chronic haemorrhagic contents, classically associated with an ovarian endometrioma.
4. How do you distinguish adenomyosis from fibroids on MRI?
5. Can MRI definitively diagnose ovarian cancer?
6. What does restricted diffusion mean?
7. What is the role of MRI in cervical cancer?
8. How can MRI distinguish a septate from a bicornuate uterus?
9. What is the role of MRI in endometriosis?
10. Is MRI safe in pregnancy?
11. What is the MRI appearance of a dermoid cyst?

13. What is the role of MRI in endometrial cancer?

Examiner: “A patient has an MRI showing multiple uterine fibroids and desires future pregnancy. What would you do?”
Model answer:

“I would first assess the patient's symptoms, age, reproductive history, fertility goals, fibroid size, number and location, particularly whether the endometrial cavity is distorted. I would investigate other causes of infertility where appropriate.

For fibroids significantly affecting the cavity or causing relevant symptoms, myomectomy may be considered after counselling about benefits, surgical risks, recurrence and future pregnancy implications. I would avoid recommending hysterectomy in a patient who wishes to preserve fertility.”
Examiner: “MRI shows an ovarian endometrioma in a woman with infertility. Should it be removed?”
Model answer:

“Not necessarily. Management depends on pain, cyst characteristics, ovarian reserve, previous surgery, accessibility for assisted reproduction and fertility plans. Surgery can reduce ovarian reserve and is not routinely performed solely to improve IVF success. I would discuss the case with an endometriosis and fertility specialist.”

content_groups.group_title: Examiner: “MRI suggests cervical cancer with parametrial invasion. What is the next step?”

blocks.text: Model answer:

“I would confirm that histological diagnosis is established, refer the patient to the gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary team and complete staging investigations as indicated. Parametrial invasion corresponds to at least FIGO stage IIB if no more advanced features are present. Definitive chemoradiation with brachytherapy is commonly recommended for this extent of disease, with treatment individualised by the oncology team.”

items: C. Macroscopic fat with signal loss on fat suppression

blocks.text: For any MRI pelvis OSCE station, aim to deliver the following in approximately 60–90 seconds:

“This is an MRI of the female pelvis. I would first identify the imaging plane and sequence, then systematically assess the uterus, cervix, ovaries, adnexa and adjacent pelvic structures. I would describe any abnormality according to its site, size, morphology, signal characteristics and local extension. I would then provide the most likely diagnosis, relevant differential diagnoses and any features suspicious for malignancy. Finally, I would correlate the findings with the patient's clinical presentation and recommend appropriate further investigations and management.”
Key examination principle: Describe what you see before stating what you think it is.

Educational note: The images are representative references rather than a single complete diagnostic MRI study. Actual MRI interpretation requires review of all relevant sequences, the formal radiology report and clinical context. Treatment should follow current local and specialist guidance.
